SCHOOLS IN JACKSON COUNTY

The first organized school in Kansas was organized in Wyandotte by J.M. Armstrong in 1844. It lasted until his death in 1852. The school had the distinction of being the first established for white children in what is now the state of Kansas. A school for whites was established in Council Grove in 1851 by Mr. T.S. Huffaker. The State of Kansas is challenged to find another county surpassing Jackson in its zealous devotion to educational matters.
Shortly after the county was organized in 1857, the people began to think about schools for their children.

The first school was taught in this county by Miss Hariet Warfield of Clay County Missouri in 1857. It was gotten up on the subscription plan, and held in a little log cabin, 10 feet square, located on the SW 1/4 section 23, township 9, range 16. This would put about 5 miles east of Hoyt. (1)
School was started in Jefferson township the same year. Mrs. H.S. Hart held school in her log cabin.
Hard times, drought, the coming of the Civil War and the internal strife in Kansas kept the people of Jackson County from doing much about schools until after 1861. (1)

The first real school was built in the county in 1858. It was built out of logs and was also used as a church. Information from the Kansas State Historical Society, says that the lighting came from leaving out one log in the wall on one side. It was heated by a fireplace. It was taught by Miss Anna Parrot. The name of it was called Brick, and was also the first organized district in county. Permission for this was granted on June 20, 1859. It was located on land which was part of the Pottawatomie Reserve. The school term was six months, three months in spring and three in the fall.

In 1868, George and Mary Hafer donated one acre of land to the school. It was about 1/2 mile west of the log cabin. In the same Brick school was built. In one porch was W.H. Webster. He taught for seven terms. At one time there were 58 students. The building was also used as a church until a church building was completed in 1890. In 1916 the second building was torn down and a building, with a basement was erected. School was held here until it was destroyed by a tornado in 1962. The last teacher was Katherin Linehan.
(The information about Brick was Kansas Historical Society and Forest Morris family and the Everett Gibson family.)
The first school in Douglas township was built in 1859. It was a

log structure, 18x20 constructed by neighbors who worked together and did an agreed part of the work. Later 'Star' was built. A group of people met Nov. S, 1859 to organize district #12. They chose the site on March 17, 1860. This located in the SE corner 1/4 of section 22, township 9, range 16. Bainbridge, RichardS and Rippitoe were names frequently mentioned.

The first school in Jefferson was taught by Mrs. H.S. Hart. Ed Hulan taught the first one in Grant township in 1858 and the first building was built in 1859. Sophia Lattimer taught the first one in Liberty township in a log house on the subscription plan. James B. Hastings was the first teacher in Straight Creek and the first building was erected in 1859.
The first school in Tippinville was taught by Miss Rioce in the winter of 1857 and 1858 in her home. One source says the building was bout 1/4 mile east of the crossroads.

Alan Gardnier states the first building made of logs, was built where the cemetery south of Denison is. A few years later a school house was built on the Claud Braum shop lots where Denison now stands.

A Log building housed the first one in Cedar township. It was built by individual subscription on S.J. Elliot's land in 1858. It later moved 1 mile south. The next was built in 1862. ( from Platt Book 1881 Cedar township. )

There were at least 14 school districts formed in 1859. They were Brick, Holton, Denison, Center, Stone (it was called Banner later), Liberty, Philo, Pleasant Valley, Lawn Ridge, Mulinax, Cedar Hill, North Star, Point Pleasant, Cedar Vale.

The first school in Holton was established in 1858 with the construction of a frame building at 415 Wisconsin. Only the lower grades maintained at that time. This continued in this building until Central was completed in 1875 at the corner of 5th and New Jersey. Prof.. C.Y. Roop organized the first high school in 1880 and the first graduation was in 1881. After the establishment of high school classes, Central School was used as as as both grade and high school. The lower grades were conducted on the lower floor and high school on the upper floor. Prof. Roop served as both superintendent and only teacher for the 3 students in first high school. Colorado school was built in 1885 at the corner of 5th & Colorado Ave. Although this school has no direct relation to the hich school, it was an internal part of the Holton school system which eventually produced high school students.
The first high school in Ho1ton was built in 1906 and continued there until 1916 when Campbell College at the north edge of Holton was acquired for use as a larger high school.

At first the county was called Calhoun. On September 24,1855 Jackson County was organized. This area went to the Kansas River. In 1868 the county was divided into two counties we do not find any mention of a superintendent until 1859. He was Ira Taber. His name is signed to the first 14 districts.

In 1860 Jackson County had population of 2,297 of which 396 were of school age, 5 to 20 years old. in 1872 this had increased to 2,587, and by 1880 to 3,855. In 1872 there were 51 districts and 6 joint districts, and by 1882, this had increased to 70 with 6 joint districts. The population was greatest around Holton. Other than that more students were in the south part of the county.

POTTAWATOMIE INDIAN MISSION AND SCHOOL
JACKSON CO., KAN.

The Pottawatomie Indian School and Mission, located on the NE 1/4 S 16, T. 9, R. 14 in Jackson County started in 1872, when a two and one half story building was completed for that purpose early in the year. The site of the school was on the summit of a high grassy hill, the building facing the north and east. This location is just a short distance east of the townsite of Nadeau which is also on the same quarter section. The town consisted of a general store and trading post run by Eli Nadeau, who was also postmaster.

The school having been built a considerable distance from a natural water supply, was supplied with that requisite by means of a pumping plant installed in the valley of Big Soldier creek on the west, which pumped water into one or more large size cisterns on the school grounds located at advantageous points.

The first building used for mission and school purposes, was 30x40 feet in size, the main school roam being 22 x 40 feet in size, thoroughly seated with desks and otherwise suitably furnished. This building was two and one-half stories high. Other buildings were added from time to time as Government funds were available and necessity demanded. After being used for a number of years the school was abandoned in l9–, the only remaining structure on the school site being a thick-walled, stone guard house which as erected to care for any recalcitrant "bucks" who paid the school visit end became obnoxious. Foundations of the rest of the

(buildings?) can still he plainly traced - having been left even with the ground. A cistern or two, covered over with old lumber are yet apparently serviceable. A few scraggly trees are lonely survivors of this once busy locality. The chapel, built for the mission, stands on the slope a short distance to the west, and faces north. It has not been used for years. In 1933, when visited by the author, was being used as a sort of granary, tool house, etc, while several swarms of bees hon also preempted quarters beneath the roof also. Beside the chapel on the west, at this time, we’re several troughs, each about 10 or 12 feet long, which had been made for the use of the Indians. These troughs were fashioned from the trunk of a large hollowed out tree. The ends were boarded up so they would hold water. One authority. commenting on these receptacles, assured the party that the squaws used them for mixing their bread dough; they were also used for watering their horses and cattle, for doing the family washings and for taking baths. A few feet away, in a chicken pen, were several wooden troughs, much smaller in size, looking as old as the troughs before mentioned. These had  served as feeding receptacles and watering troughs for small pigs and poultry. While showing signs of disintegration, they looked good for a number of years service still.

Eli Nadeau had conducted a large and well stocked trading post or the Pottawatomie on be reservation for many years, on the prairie slope just to the southwest of the mission, facing upon a trail running to the south.
Nadeau was a tall, dark, squarely-built business man, the summer of 1897,

and at that time was probably between 65 and 70 years of age. Under the treaties of 1866 and 1867, between the Government and the Prairie Band or the Pottawatomie Nation, he became one of the "Business Committee" of the tribe, for the purpose of listing the members and fixing their family relations by family units, ages and names of members.

The other two members of this committee were George Young and William W. Ross. Young was a white man, formerly a citizen of Kentucky, who had become the husband of a French and Pottawatomie woman, and thus a member of the tribe. He was the father of Mrs. Frank Bourbonais, now residing upon her allotment west of the old mission, on the NW 1/4, S. 17, T. 9, R. 14 and grandfather of Mrs. OSHA Wyatt, now residing upon her allotment just across the highway west on the NW 1/4, S.18, T. 9, R. 14. William W.
Ross the other member was a white man, and reputed to be the Ross for whom the village of Roseville was named.

Under the provisions of the treaty of 1867, Nadeau went through the proceedings in the Federal court, and became a naturalized citizen, for a few months, thereafter he secured an order of that court returning him to the status of a blanket Indian. One of his sons, Joseph E. Nadeau, by his friends called "Coe" Nadeau, owns and resides upon a well improved fore facing south on the north side of Highway No.40 just in the west edge of Shawnee county, on the SE 1/4, S. 13, T. 10, R. 12, and like his father, reputed to he e vary good and conservative business man.

Eli passed away in Oklahoma, about____, possibly in the neighborhood of the inland village of Burnett, (named for Joseph Burnett, son of the noted Chief Abram(?) Burnett), located in the old Pottawatomie Reserve, near Shawnee(?), Oklahoma.

Too high an estimate cannot be placed on the religious, moral and practically useful influences of these schools. They not only bring the children in contact with religious and cultivated persons, but through them reach their parents and friends, who visit them. The improved health and deportment of their children and their ability to read, write, and figure for them has convinced the adults that their children are learning that which makes the white race powerful, and their affection for those placed in charge of them is a proof that they are kindly treated. Through the schools the adult Indians have learned that a regard for virtue has its reward in the respect entertained for those who practice it, and that no good thing is expected from an untruthful or immoral source. Though we do not obtain actual expressions of religious conviction, I have not a doubt but that these influences are gradually enlightening the Indians to a better conception of true religion.

Until three years ago the Prairie band had not sent their children to school or had the advantages of religious instruction, or even example, no agent or missionary having resided among them. Living within a short distance of religious white communities and almost in hearing of church-bells, they isolated themselves from the balance of their own people, and were strangers to the voices of friend-ship and advice. Hence, while within reach of inestimable knowledge, the cultivated and cherished those religious traditions and customs which deepened in their minds a dislike of revealed religion, and prejudice against those who taught it. To be learned in these traditions was a position of honor: therefore it will not seem strange that the ablest and best informed men in the tribe made these subjects

their Greatest study. These men are generally practical on other subjects, but introduce religious questions, and they become adamant. They say, "We have the Knowledge that we must hold to our belief until our Savious comes and redeems us: that any deviation or departure from it will delay his coming." This belief must be persistently attacked. To overthrow it is not the work of a month or a year. It requires incessant and prudent effort through every individual brought in contact with them in every business transaction and through every influence that can be exerted. By pursuing this course, a modification of their extreme views has already been accomplished, and when the school children, with their changed habits and different views, commence to move among them in the discharge of the duties of life, their influence, in addition to other agencies, will, I have no doubt, hasten the consummation of our hope that these Indians will accept the religion of our Saviour Jesus Christ.
M. H. NEWLIN, United States Indian Agent.
William Nicholson, Superintendent of Indian Affairs, Lawrence, Kansas.

The pioneer schools, were held in rudely constructed log houses and provided with homemade furniture, the seats being made of puncheon, with wooden pegs for legs, and wooden pegs were driven into the wall to support a board which served as a desk for the pupils to write upon.

DENISON RURAL HIGH SCHOOL
V.J. Cramer, Principal

Denison high school dates back to 1908 when an additional year of schooling was added to the school system of Denison. A part of the grade school building was used and there was only one teacher who offered four subjects: algebra, ancient history, Latin and English to the 50 pupils who were enrolled that year. At the end of the school year, these 50 pupils were wanting more knowledge and were urging that another year be added to the high school course. Thus Denison high school became a two year school and remained so until 1915 when, in accordance with advancing times and the need for still more education, another year was added.

By that time there were more classes and a greater number of students in the high school and that necessitated more room. The crowded conditions at the school was not conducive to the best work so some of the public-spirited citizens of Denison began to agitate the question of a new building. Everyone realize that a building was needed, but some felt that the community could not carry the extra burden which a new building would mean.

In 1916 the fourth year of the course was added, and now with still more subjects being offered and a still greater number of pupils coming in, something had to be done. Someone believed that the aim of a new building might be reached by means of the new rural high school system and by 1917, the New Denison Rural High School was started on the road to success. In 1918 the building was completed and school begin in it in September.
Denison Rural High School claims the honor of being the second rural high school in Jackson County.

However, though it is one of the oldest, it is still one of the best in the county., since it was well-made and has been well taken care of. Much of the credit for the latter must be given to Mr. C. E. Brown, who has kept the building in excellent condition for all about two years since its erection. In the building there are: a gymnasium, an auditorium, study hall, a good library, five recitation rooms, laboratories and each room as well equipped.

Denison High School ranks among the highest in the county and the community and students are proud of the fact that it was rated 100% in 1928. The students always make a good showing in athletic and intellectual contest and their eagerness to do so is attributed to the "old school spirit"-that fine attitude and feeling prevailing in D.R.H.S. which makes the student feel that he cannot give less than his best whatever the contest.

Pleasant Valley #8
March 21, 1986
Dear Mr. Copeland,

/tI read any recent issue of the Holton recorder in the column by Doris Shoff, that you would like pictures or history of one room schools in Jackson County. I know that you lack either a picture or history of several schools, including Pleasant Valley, district # 8. Recently I sent a picture of that school in care of Gladys Riley so I expect you have received it by this time.

As to some history of the school, I do not know when the school located at 7 miles west of Holton was built, but I know it was previous to the year 1907 as that was the year I first attended that school, along with two of my sisters. I remember that Fisher Stauffer was a member of the school board (Mr. Stauffer was the paternal grandfather of Auswell, Thane and Lauren Stauffer) and one time after the school board had purchased and installed new desks throughout the one room, Mr. Stauffer delivered a lecture to the students about the care that should be taken of the new desks. As a parking suggestion, he said "anyone doing any carving on the new desk should be yanked out of his seat and thumped for 26 minutes." As I said, I do not know what year the school at that location was built, but I do remember my father, Ev McDonald, telling we children that previous to the building of the new school, he had attended a one room school, which was located about 1/2 mile east of the new school on the south side of the road on a part of the farm owned and occupied by the Hearn family, later the John Fisher farm, which is now owned and occupied by Fred Fischer and wife. My father told us that he remembered Elizabeth Hearn attending that school, said that she was such a tiny, dainty little girl.

There are many incidents that I remember in connection with dear Pleasant Valley school, but one I especially remember, was in connection with a custom of those days in country schools. It was such fun to go home with special friends to spend the night and one time I had gone home with a special friend and at the "supper" table that evening, the large bowl of fried potatoes was passed to me first. well, my friend had a small brother at home, not yet school age and when I was handed the dish, he said to me "don’t you take all the Brown tatie’s!". I do not remember whether or not he was reprimanded, but I think I shall never forget the incident!
Yours truly,
Evelyn (McDonald) LaMar

Prior to 1858, the schools of the county were maintained by subscription or private enterprise. In 1857 the first school in Douglas Township was taught by Miss Harriet Warfield of Clay, Missouri, on the subscription plan. She was the niece of A. S. Cambridge. Bainbridge was director, John Rippetoe clerk, and J.J. Grooling was treasurer, John Rippetoe may be entitled to be named the founding father. School house was built at logs in 1858, 16 ft.² in area and located on the southwest quarter of section 23, town 9, Range 16. This is the same location where the first Star school was built in 1859.

Original Star school # 12 was organized 11–5–1859. Star district in 1885 had an enrollment of 84 pupils, so they divided it into two districts in 1886. South Star # 76 and Star # 12 became Northstar. North Star retained the old Star # 12. After the school was closed it was still used by the Muddy Creek Baptist Church for their services until they built their church in 1895.
North Star (Star) disorganized and consolidated with South Star on 3–13–1952, at that time South Star’s name was changed to Star. Star (South Star) voluntarily disorganized 8–2–1962.

Northstar number 12 was organized November 5, 1859. According to the minutes of the organizational meeting, the meeting was held in the Point Pleasant school. The minutes up to March 27, 1872 call it Point Pleasant. After then, they read Star. It was located on the S east corner, Southwest 1/4 – 22–9 South. Alpheus Bainbridge, chairman; Alfred Richards, clerk.
A new building was built in 1886. Due to population increase, the district split and South Star was built (district 76.) In 1885 there were 84 pupils in Star.
Point Pleasant # 13
The records show Point Pleasant was organized in 1859. This was apparently Star # 12. Due to increase in population the district split.

Point Pleasant number 13 was organized September 20, 1873. It was located Northwest corner north east 1/4, 9 – 9–16 E. The first building burned, the second was taken by a tornado in 1916, the third still stands.
The record attendance was 55 and 1885. The teacher was Maggie Robson. Her salary was $40.
Cedar Vale #14
tCedar Vale #14: It was organized in 1859. It was 2 miles north of Marietta in the N E corner of the NE 1/4 of SE 1/4 of 10 – 8– 15 east(?). This building was built in 1901.
This picture was donated by Shelby Campbell. They lived half mile west and north of the school. He later served on the school board is treasurer during 1934 to 37 years.
Mrs. Iola book James taught their 1919 and 1920. Mrs. James is the mother of Mary Robb.
